Correlation V. Causation

Correlation implies a linear association between two variables. 
library(tidyverse)
library(estimatr)
library(patchwork)

anscombe_tidy <- anscombe %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c(".value", "set"),
    names_pattern = "(.)(.)"
  ) %>%
  mutate(set = case_when(set == 1 ~ "1. Linear", set == 2 ~ "2. Non-Linear", set == 3 ~ "3. Outlier", set == 4 ~ "4. High Leverage"))


ggplot(anscombe_tidy, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Anscombe's Quartet",
       subtitle = "Linear Associations and Best Fits",
       x = "X",
       y = "Y") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())+
  facet_wrap(~set, ncol = 2)

Causation refers to the idea that some variable \(X\) is responsible for changes in another variable \(Y\). “\(X\) is doing something to \(Y\)”. Alternatively, “\(X\) causes \(Y\) if, were we to intervene and change the value of \(X\), then the distribution of \(Y\) would also change as a result.” (Huntington-Klein 2022: 89)

Correlation may not imply causation because:

  1. Causal relationships can exist even when there is no observable correlation between two variables (see Panel B).
set.seed(2025)

dat_correlation <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(1000, mean = 0, sd = 1),
  y = x + rnorm(1000, mean = 0.5, sd = 1),
  y2 = x ^ 2
)

fig1 = ggplot(data = dat_correlation, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm_robust", se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("(A) Linear Association") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)

fig2 = ggplot(data = dat_correlation, aes(x = x, y = y2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm_robust", se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("(B) Non-Linear Association") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)

fig1 + fig2

  1. A causal relationship may not exist even when there is correlation (or association) between variables.

Example: Does attending a SAT preparation course cause an improvement in SAT scores? Attendance may be correlated with higher scores but confounded by other factors like motivation and affluence (more affluent or motivated students may be more likely to enroll in preparatory course and more likely to score higher on the test).

Figure 1: DAGs and Confounding

A directed acyclic graph (“DAG”) is a visual depiction of empirical associations. In the above example, attendance in preparatory classes (\(X\)) is associated with higher test scores (\(Y\)) but other confounding factors (motivation and affluence) affect \(X\) and \(Y\). There is an unblocked backdoor path connecting \(X\) and \(Y\), potentially confounding the association between these variables.

Experiments and Confounding

Experiments randomly assign subjects to get an intervention (treatment group) or not (control group). The promise of this design is that “observed and unobserved factors that affect outcomes are equally likely to be present in the treatment and control groups” (FEDAI:8)

Put another way, “[t]he procedure of assigning treatments at random ensures that there is no systematic tendency for either the treatment or control group to have an advantage” (FEDAI:7)

Figure 2: Experiments Deal With Confounding

Types of Experiments

Experiments can be conducted in laboratory settings, embedded in surveys, or fielded in the real world.

A natural experiment is one in which someone other than the researcher (say a government) randomly assigns treatment.

A quasi experiment is when treatment is as-if randomly or plausibly randomly assigned. Note, someone (researcher or otherwise) did not actually randomly assign subjects to treatments. The process of assignment is “near-random”.

In an experiment, the researcher controls and determines the assignment of subjects to treatment(s).

A field experiment is an experiment that is: (i) conducted in a real world setting; (ii) involves participants that “resemble the actors who ordinarily encounter the intervention” (FEDAI:10); (iii) uses a treatment that “resembles the intervention of interest in the world” (FEDAI:10); and (iv) has outcomes that “resemble actual outcomes of theoretical or practical interest” (FEDAI:11).

**Evaluating “Fieldness”: Context, Content, Participants, Outcomes.

Note: Random sampling is not the same as random assignment of treatment. Random sampling refers to the process by which subjects are selected into a study. It guarantees representativeness. Random assignment refers to how selected subjects are assigned to treatment(s). It deals with confounding. A randomly selected sample that is non-randomly assigned to treatment does not deal with confounding.

Exercise

Identify the best research design to study each of the following research questions. You may use Claude or ChatGPT to brainstorm ideas.

  1. What political views do “moderates” hold in America?

  2. Does incumbency affect re-election prospects in future elections?

  3. Does compulsory voting increase citizens’ political engagement?

  4. Does exposure to globalization increase support for populist parties?

  5. Why does ethnic diversity undermine the provision of public goods?
